[ASSISTANT_SAID] The Boltzmann constant is expressed in terms of joules per kelvin (J/K) and relates the temperature of a system to the average kinetic energy of its particles.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The Boltzmann constant is defined as: k = 1/N * (1/2m) * ∑(mv^2), where k is the Boltzmann constant, N is the number of particles, m is the mass of each particle, and ∑(mv^2) is the sum of the kinetic energy of all particles.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The Boltzmann constant is fundamental in statistical mechanics and has applications in thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and statistical physics.  
[USER] Summarizing your last few answers, it would be fair to say that the only things we deem to be constant in the observable universe are the ratios of variables but is there anything that is simply constant, with only one unit of measurement involved?  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Some physical constants are considered to be constants in the observable universe, including both ratios of two quantities and independent constants with their own units of measurement.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Examples of ratio constants include the speed of light (c), the gravitational constant (G), and the Coulomb constant (k).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Examples of independent constants include the Planck constant (h), the electron charge (e), and the mass of the proton (mp).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The Planck constant has a value of approximately 6.63 x 10^-34 joule-seconds (J-s).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The electron charge has a value of approximately 1.60 x 10^-19 coulombs (C).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The mass of the proton has a value of approximately 1.67 x 10^-27 kilograms (kg).  
[USER] Ok so charges and mass of particular particles are fixed but everything else is expressed as a ratio or product of two other measures?  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Yes, charges and masses of particular particles are fixed constants, while many other physical quantities are expressed as ratios or products of two other measures.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The speed of light (c) is the ratio of distance traveled to time taken, the gravitational constant (G) is the ratio of force of gravity to the product of masses and distance squared, and the Coulomb constant (k) is the ratio of electrostatic force to the product of charges and distance squared.
